title: Optimizer Comparison Quiz
description: Test your understanding of optimization algorithms

questions.question: What is the main limitation of basic SGD that momentum addresses?
options: SGD is too slow to compute
SGD oscillates in ravines and converges slowly
questions.explanation: Basic SGD can oscillate back and forth across narrow valleys (ravines) and converge slowly because it only considers the current gradient. Momentum addresses this by accumulating gradients over time, building up velocity in consistent directions and dampening oscillations.

questions.question: How does momentum help optimization?
options: It reduces the learning rate automatically
It accumulates gradients to accelerate in consistent directions
It requires less memory than SGD
questions.explanation: Momentum works like a ball rolling downhill - it accumulates velocity (gradients) over time. This accelerates movement in directions where gradients consistently point the same way, while dampening oscillations where gradients alternate. The result is faster convergence and smoother trajectories.

questions.question: What problem does RMSProp solve that AdaGrad has?
options: RMSProp prevents the learning rate from decaying too aggressively
questions.explanation: AdaGrad accumulates all squared gradients throughout training, causing the learning rate to monotonically decrease and eventually become too small. RMSProp fixes this by using an exponential moving average of squared gradients, which 'forgets' old gradients and allows the learning rate to increase again if needed.

questions.question: What does Adam combine?
questions.explanation: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) combines the best of both worlds: momentum (first moment - mean of gradients) for acceleration and RMSProp (second moment - variance of gradients) for adaptive learning rates. This combination makes Adam robust and effective across many problems.

questions.question: What are typical default values for Adam's hyperparameters?
questions.explanation: The standard default hyperparameters for Adam are: learning rate α=0.001, β₁=0.9 (first moment decay), and β₂=0.999 (second moment decay). These defaults work well for many problems, which is one reason Adam is so popular - it requires minimal tuning.

questions.question: Why does Adam use bias correction in early iterations?
options: To correct for the initialization bias toward zero
questions.explanation: Adam initializes the first and second moment estimates (m and v) to zero. In early iterations, these estimates are biased toward zero. Bias correction (dividing by 1-β^t) compensates for this initialization bias, ensuring accurate estimates even in the first few iterations. As training progresses, the correction becomes negligible.

questions.question: Which optimizer typically converges fastest with minimal tuning?
questions.explanation: Adam typically converges fastest with minimal hyperparameter tuning because it combines momentum for acceleration with adaptive learning rates for per-parameter optimization. Its default hyperparameters work well across many problems, making it an excellent choice for quick prototyping and when you don't have time for extensive tuning.

questions.question: When might you prefer SGD with momentum over Adam?
options: When you want better generalization and have time to tune hyperparameters
When you're working with sparse data
questions.explanation: While Adam converges faster, well-tuned SGD with momentum sometimes achieves better generalization (test performance). If you have time to carefully tune the learning rate and momentum, and you're training from scratch on large datasets, SGD with momentum can be the better choice. Many state-of-the-art results use carefully tuned SGD.

questions.question: What does the momentum coefficient β control?
options: How much past gradients influence current updates
questions.explanation: The momentum coefficient β (typically 0.9) controls how much past gradients influence the current update. A value of 0.9 means the velocity retains 90% of its previous value and adds 10% of the current gradient. Higher β means more smoothing and longer 'memory' of past gradients.

questions.question: Which optimizer is best suited for problems with very sparse features?
questions.explanation: AdaGrad and Adam are well-suited for sparse features because they adapt the learning rate per parameter. Rare features (which have infrequent, sparse gradients) get larger effective learning rates, allowing them to learn more when they do appear. This is particularly useful in NLP and recommendation systems with sparse data.

questions.question: True or False: Adam always achieves better test accuracy than SGD with momentum.
questions.explanation: False. While Adam typically converges faster during training, well-tuned SGD with momentum sometimes achieves better generalization (test accuracy). Adam may converge to sharper minima that don't generalize as well. The choice depends on the problem, and both optimizers have their place in practice.

questions.question: True or False: RMSProp uses an exponential moving average of squared gradients instead of accumulating all history like AdaGrad.
questions.explanation: True. This is the key difference between RMSProp and AdaGrad. RMSProp uses an exponential moving average (with decay rate β, typically 0.9) which gives more weight to recent gradients and 'forgets' old ones. This prevents the learning rate from decaying too aggressively, which was AdaGrad's main limitation.
